problems.title: Problem 9.1(a) — original
problems.source: Original user-uploaded Chapter9 textbook Problems9.1–9.5 verbatim, expressly UNSOLVED
problems.prompt:
Assume that Debtor has a total of $20,000 in unsecured claims when it files bankruptcy. Three years prior to filing bankruptcy, Debtor made a constructively fraudulent transfer of property worth $18,000 to Party X. The only remaining creditor in the bankruptcy with standing to avoid the transfer to X under the state fraudulent transfer law is Creditor A (who had a present claim at the time of the transfer to X). A's claim is $100. The rest of the Debtor's creditors, with total claims of $19,900, had future claims and thus could not avoid the transfer to X under state law.

Debtor's bankruptcy trustee sues to avoid the transfer to X under § 544(b).

a. In what amount will the trustee be able to set aside the transfer to X?

problems.title: Problem 9.2(c) — original
problems.source: Original user-uploaded Chapter9 textbook Problems9.1–9.5 verbatim, expressly UNSOLVED
problems.prompt:
Reference facts from part (a):

May the trustee avoid any of the following under § 544(a)(1)?

c. Assume the same facts as in a., except that on May 1 Debtor granted Creditor a mortgage in real property worth $10,000 to secure a $10,000 debt, and Creditor had not recorded the mortgage in the real property records by May 10, when Debtor filed chapter 7. Under state law, a bona fide purchaser for value without actual knowledge of an unrecorded conveyance of real estate would take free of that conveyance, but a judgment creditor that obtains a judicial lien on a debtor's real property is not considered a bona fide purchaser.

problems.title: Problem 9.4(a) — original
problems.source: Original user-uploaded Chapter9 textbook Problems9.1–9.5 verbatim, expressly UNSOLVED
problems.prompt:
Which of the following constitutes an actually fraudulent transfer? In which will the transferee be protected from recovery?

a. Debtor owes 10 creditors $50,000, and is in default on 7 of the debts. Five creditors bring lawsuits against the Debtor. Debtor's only nonexempt asset is a valuable painting she inherited from her father, worth $40,000. Debtor sells the painting to Art Mann, a wealthy collector, for $38,000. Art Mann knows nothing of Debtor's financial situation. Debtor deposits the cash in her bank, wire transfers the money to a Swiss bank, and disappears. Two months later, an involuntary chapter 7 order for relief is entered against Debtor.

problems.title: Problem 9.5(a) — original
problems.source: Original user-uploaded Chapter9 textbook Problems9.1–9.5 verbatim, expressly UNSOLVED
problems.prompt: a. Nine years ago, Debtor was planning to start a new commercial real estate business as a sole proprietorship. At the time, he had debts of $500,000 and assets of $1,000,000. He had no lawsuits pending against him. His projected income statements showed a net positive monthly cash flow of $90,000 (expenses of $150,000, income of $240,000). However, the income projection depended on Debtor accurately predicting commercial rental and occupancy rates. Debtor had spent the last 20 years working in the commercial real estate field. Recognizing the inherent riskiness of his business plan, Debtor transferred $500,000 to an asset protection trust in the Cook Islands. Debtor was the sole beneficiary of this trust. For several years, his business worked well. However, commercial rental and occupancy rates fell dramatically last year. Debtor, unfortunately, had made a big investment predicting a steady increase in commercial rental and occupancy rates. Debtor filed chapter 7 bankruptcy last month. At the time of filing, Debtor had assets of $2,500,000 and debts of $9,000,000. The trustee brought suit to avoid the transfer to the Cook Islands trust nine years ago. What result?
